Need to promote and celebrate the Jagannath Temple in Digha as  
a major pilgrimage and Cultural Centre 
SHRIMATI SAGARIKA GHOSE (West Bengal) : Sir, Lord Jagannath Temple in Digha 
is not merely a structure of brick and mortar . It is a beacon of a civilization, a culture 
and a philosophy of faith that Bengal has nurtured for centuries. Inaugurated less than 
a year ago, built in a majestic Kalinga ar chitectural style, the temple has already 
drawn nearly one crore visitors from more than 150 countries. On Akshay Tritiya, April 
[ 11 March, 2026 ]
7

30, 2025, Bengal opened the gates of the Jagannath Temple, 213 feet of devotion 
rising from the shores of the Bay of Beng al, and the people responded.  There were 
one crore devotees in just eight months. Nearly 50,000 pilgrims visit every day, turning 
what was once a quiet seaside town into one of India's fastest rising spiritual 
destinations. Hotels are full, livelihoods are growing and the local economy is thriving.   
(MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair.) 
This is people's faith in motion. Th is is not propaganda. This is pure bhakti. It 
is not a temple built to divide, intimidate  or score political points. Bengal said 
something very simple and very profound. We do not weaponize faith. We live it. 
Across our land, across Bengal, stand the symb ols of pluralism, the tomb of Mother 
Teresa, Nakhoda Masjid, Belur Math and ISCKON temple. Azan and temple bells, 
keertan and qawwali,  sufi, buddhist, sikh, all coexist in Bengal’s spiritual vibrancy, 
because Bengal is the land of Rama krishna Paramhansa who taught us ‘ jato mat 
thatho path’, ‘many roads, one God’.  Bengal is the land of Chaitanya Mahaprabhu 
whose message teaches us ‘humbler than gra ss, more tolerant than a tree’.  Bengal 
is the land of Swami Vivekananda who warned us that while superstition may be the 
great enemy of man, bigotry is far worse. Be ngal is the land of  Rabindranath Tagore 
who reminded us that the world is a united stream of life. For centuries our philosophy 
has echoed the ancient truth - Ekam Sat Vipra Bahudha Vadanti ; truth is one, the 
wise call it many names.  An d that truth is lived in Beng al every day. The Jagannath 
temple in Digha welcomes ev ery caste, every creed, every community; it is open and 
inclusive, without gate-keeping. Our Chief Minister's words capture perfectly 21 st 
century modern secularism – dharma jar jar, utsab shabar  – which means, 
everybody has their personal religion, bu t we celebrate festivals together. The

Devolution of funds in Panchayati Raj Institutions 
*196. SHRI RAGHAV CHADHA : Will the Minister of PANCHAYATI RAJ  be pleased to 
state: 
	(a)  whether Government has assessed the status of devolution of funds, 
functions and functionaries to Pancha yati Raj Institutions in the recent 
years and if so, the details thereof; 
(b)    the number of States that have  completed activity mapping and devolution 
of the funds, functions and functionaries, details thereof; 
(c)    what steps are being taken by Gove rnment to ensure effective devolution to 
Panchayats, the details thereof; and 
(d)    the outcomes of the steps taken by Government in strengthening local self-
governance, State-wise and year-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (PROF. S. P. 
SINGH BAGHEL): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement	 
(a) to (d)   “Panchayat”, being “ Local Government”, is a State subject and 
part of State List of Seventh Schedule of th e Constitution of India. Panchayats are set 
up and operate through the respective State Panchayati Raj Acts. States have made 
their own Panchayati Raj Act, subject to the provisions of the Constitution. Article 
243G of the Constitution empowers the Legisl ature of a State to make provisions, by 
law, for the devolution of power and responsibilities upon Panchayat at appropriate 
level, subject to such conditions as may be  specified, with respect to the preparation 
of plans for economic development and social justice and implementation of schemes 
for economic development and social justice as may be entrusted to them including 
those in relation to matters listed in the Eleventh Schedule to the Constitution. The 
State legislatures are to consider the 29 su bjects listed in the Eleventh Schedule for 
devolution of power and responsibilities upon  Panchayats. Accordingly, the status of 
devolution of funds, functi ons and functionaries to Pa nchayati Raj Institutions 
depends on the extent of powers and resources devolved to them by the States 
concerned, which varies across States.

However, the Ministry of Panchayati Ra j reviews performance of Panchayats, 
from time to time, through studies, review  meetings, field visits, video conferencing, 
Information Technology applications etc.  
The Ministry has released a report titled “Status of Devolution to Panchayats in 
States - An Indicative Evidence-Based Ranking, 2024” in February 2025 to assess the 
effectiveness of devolution and the role  of local governments  in strengthening 
grassroots democracy. This report presents the Devolution Index, which provides the 
overall scores and ranks for all States/Union  Territories covered under Part-IX of the 
Constitution, based on six identified dimensions: Framework, Functions, Finances, 
Functionaries, Capacity Enhancement, and Accountability. Ranking of States/UTs in 
Devolution Index and Sub-indices is attached as Annexure-I.  
  To strengthen the local self-governance framework of Panchayati Raj 
Institutions across the country, this  Ministry has launched eGramSwaraj 
(https://egramswaraj.gov.in), a user friendly  web-based portal, which aims to bring 
in better transparency in th e decentralized planning, progress reporting, financial 
management, work-based accounting an d details of assets created. The 
eGramSwaraj portal has also been integr ated with Public Financial Management 
System for online transfer of the Central Finance Commission funds by the States to 
PRIs and enabling Panchayats to make real-time payments to vendors/service 
providers. Panchayats prepare and uplo ad their Annual Panchayat Development 
Plans on eGramSwaraj portal. In addition , the Ministry has integrated eGramSwaraj 
with the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) to bring transparency to Panchayat 
procurement.  The status of adoption of  eGramSwaraj under XV Finance Commission 
for the year 2025-26 by States and status  of Panchayat Development Plans are at 
Annexure-II & Annexure-III respectively.  
The Ministry has implemented Mission Mode Project on e-Panchayats (MMP-
ePanchayat), a Central component of the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA) 
scheme under which various e-governance projects are funded towards digitalization 
of Panchayats. Revamped Centrally Sponsored Scheme of RGSA has been 
implemented w.e.f. financial year 2022-23 in States/ Union Territories with main 
objective for capacitating PRIs through imparting training to all the Elected 
Representatives, functionaries and other stakeholders to develop their governance 
capabilities for leadersh ip roles to enable the Panchaya ts to function effectively. 
Under the scheme, Ministry supplements the efforts of States/UTs on limited scale for 
creation basic infrastructure for effective functioning of Gram Panchayats such as

Demand for inclusion of tenant farmers from Goa under PM-KISAN  
Samman Nidhi Scheme 
SHRI SADANAND MHALU SHET TANAVADE (Goa):  Madam, I draw attention of the 
Government to the urgent need for inclus ion of tenant farmers from Goa under the 
PM-KISAN Samman Nidhi Scheme. This flagship initiative of the Government of India 
has been transformative for farmers acro ss the country, providing crucial income 
support, and has been widely appreciated. Goa has approximately 52,000 cultivating 
farmers. However, due to the existing elig ibility condition requiring land ownership, 
only about 6,000 farmers in the State curr ently benefit from the scheme. Under the 
Goa Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1964, tenant  cultivators enjoy rights equivalent to 
landowners for cultivation. They are treat ed as deemed owners  under State law and 
are eligible for several Stat e agricultural schemes. Currently, over 20,000 farmers in 
Goa are registered as tenant farmers, inheri tors of tenants, or in similar categories. 
Inclusion of these tenant farmers under PM-KISAN would significantly broaden the 
scheme’s reach, benefiting a large number of  small and marginal farmers, who form 
more than 80 percent of Goa’s agricu ltural community. For them, the annual 
assistance of Rs. 6,000 is vital to cover in put costs and cope with distress situations. 
Agriculture in Goa is not only critical for food security but also preserves the State’s 
natural landscape, which supports its tourism-driven economy. I request the 
Government to kindly approve the inclusio n of tenant farmers from Goa under the 
PM-KISAN scheme, so that all deserving cultivators get the support they need.

Demand for setting up AIIMS in Kozhikode, Kerala 
DR. JOHN BRITTAS (Kerala): Madam, Vice-Chairperson, in an effort to address 
regional disparities in the accessibility and affordability of advanced tertiary healthcare 
services across the nation, Government has been establishing new AIIMSs in various 
States under Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Sura ksha Yojana (PMSSY) Initiative. A total 
of 22 AIIMS have been announ ced so far under PMSSY in various States. Kerala is, 
perhaps, the only major State that does not have an AIIMS. The demand to set up an 
AIIMS in Kerala dates back over a decade. Despite Kerala's remarkable achievements 
in healthcare, it lacks a Union Government-f unded institution of national Importance 
for tertiary healthcare and res earch. Kerala identified Kinalu r in Kozhikode district as 
the proposed site for AIIMS, which is having all required facilities to cater to the 
requirements for establishment of AIIMS, and formally communicated the same to 
Centre requesting sanction. In answers to written Questions raised by me in Rajya 
Sabha on 25.07.2023 and 03.12.2024, Government revealed that the proposal for 
AIIMS in Kerala has not been approved under the current phase of PMSSY. However, 
the Minister of Health and Family Welfare had assured in Rajya Sabha, during its 265 th 
Session, that Kerala is being considered for setting up an AIIMS. Therefore, I 
earnestly urge upon the Government to  expeditiously grant approval for the 
establishment of AIIMS at Kinalur in Kozhikode district in Kerala.

Demand for inclusion of Alandi under the Temple Town  
Development Framework 
DR. MEDHA VISHRAM KULKARNI (Maharashtra) : Madam, Vice-Chairperson, I 
demand for the inclusion of Alandi, the sacred temple town of Marathi Sant 
Dnyaneshwar Maharaj in Pune district , Maharashtra, under the Temple Town 
Development framework announced by the Un ion Government. Alandi is one of the 
most revered pilgrimage centres in the country and holds exceptional spiritual, 
cultural and historical importance. It wi tnesses the arrival of lakhs of devotees 
annually, particularly during the Ashadhi and Kartiki Wari, placing immense pressure 
on civic infrastructure, sanitation, tr affic management, public amenities and 
142

environmental resources. Despite its national  spiritual significance, Alandi continues 
to face serious challenges arising from  unplanned urbanisation and inadequate 
infrastructure. The recent Union Budget’s emphasis on strengthening infrastructure in 
temple towns and Tier-II cities provides a timely and appropriate policy opportunity to 
address these long-standing issues. Inclusio n of Alandi under this framework will 
enable focused investments in pilgrim fac ilities, sanitation, sewage and solid waste 
management, riverfront development, flood co ntrol, public transport, parking, road 
connectivity and heritage conservation. Further, Alandi’s identity is inseparably linked 
with the Indrayani River, which requires ur gent rejuvenation and pollution control. 
Temple town status will facilitate integrated  planning for river restoration, alongside 
urban development, ensuring environmental sustainability and public health. 
I, therefore, urge the Government to formally include Alandi under the Temple 
Town Development Programme, so that its spiritual legacy is preserved while 
ensuring modern infrastructure, improved qu ality of life for residents and a dignified 
experience for pilgrims from across the country.

India’s social security coverage has incr eased from 19% in 2015 to 64.3% in 2025. 
India’s expansion in social protection co verage has been enabled by a strong 
foundation of digital and financial inclusion. 
  In order to extend social security be nefits to the workers in the unorganised 
sector, the Central Governme nt has launched the eShram  Portal on 26.08.2021 for 
creation of a National Database of Unorganised Workers (NDUW) seeded with 
Aadhaar. As on date, more than 31 crore unorganised workers have registered on a 
self-declaration basis in the eShram portal, which facilitates access to various social 
security and welfare schemes.

schemes implemented by the Government. Major schemes include the following:

(ii)  National Pension Scheme for Traders and Self-Employed Persons (NPS-
Traders)

Ministries/Departments, workers in the un organised sector are provided pension 
security, life and accident insurance, and health protection.

(a) to (d) The Ministry of Culture through National Mission on Libraries (NML) 
Scheme, under its ‘Setting up of NML Model Library’ component, provides financial 
assistance to one State Central Library and one District Library in each State /UT on 
the recommendation of the Stat e Authorities concerned and 6 Libraries identified by 
Ministry of Culture. The financial assistan ce is provided for i) Up-gradation of 
Infrastructure, ii) Modernization of Tec hnology & Modernization of Services, iii) 
Creation of Facilities for Specially abled us ers and iv) Subscription of E-journals/E-
books for selected Libraries under NML, v) Network Connectivity for District Libraries, 
vi) Procurement of Reading resources an d Advocacy & Outreach programs etc. The 
details of financial assistance provided to State /UT under NML during the last three 
years are given at Annexure-A. 
The Indian Culture Portal (ICP) provides a unified digital platform offering 
access to diverse cultural and knowledg e resources from across the country by 
enabling online access to curated and original  content. It promotes and showcases 
both the tangible and intangible cultural heritage of India through various categories 
which include manuscripts, museum artifacts,  paintings, archival photographs, food 
and culture, musical instruments of India,  archival documents, social practices, 
rituals, and festivals, Oral traditions and expressions and rare books, etc. These 
details are provided for every region of India and from Indus Valley Civilization to the 
present.  
The Capacity Building Programmes (CBP ) are also organized under the NML 
across the Country to provide training to lib rary professionals of all States/UTs. Till 
date 54 number of CBP have been organi zed and 2465 library professional have been 
trained.

SHRI DORJEE TSHERING LEPCHA (Sikkim): Sir, I draw attention of the Government 
towards the need for revival and strengthening of large cardamom cultivation in the 
State of Sikkim, which has long been known as the traditional home of this valuable 
spice. Large cardamom is not only an impo rtant cash crop but also a major source of 
livelihood for thousands of small and marginal farmers in the Himalayan region. 
In recent years, the production of la rge cardamom in Sikkim has declined 
significantly due to several challenges, su ch as plant diseases, climate variability, 
aging plantations and lack of adequate scientific support. This decline has directly 
affected the income and economic security of farmers, who depend heavily on this 
crop.

The Board has been implementing various schemes for the development of 
cardamom cultivation, including replantation, quality planting material distribution and 
technical training for farmers. However, th ere is a need to further strengthen these 
interventions specifically for Sikkim, considering the unique agro-climatic conditions 
of the State.

Need to enhance allo cation under MPLADS  
SHRI MASTHAN RAO YADAV BEEDHA  (Andhra Pradesh):  Sir, I seek to raise an 
important issue concerning the Members of Parliament Local Area Development 
Scheme (MPLADS), which is a vital instru ment for addressing local developmental 
needs. At present, each Member of Parliament is allocated Rs. 5 crore per year under 
the MPLADS. However, the effective valu e of development works executed on the 
ground is considerably reduced due to stat utory deductions such as GST at 18 per 
cent, seigniorage charges of around 5 pe r cent, quality control charges and other 
mandatory recoveries during implementation. As a result, the actual developmental 
output comes down to nearly 75 per cent of the sanctioned amount. Consequently, 
from the nominal allocation of Rs. 5 crore, the real value of works executed is only 
about Rs. 3.5 to Rs. 3.75 crore. This limi ts the ability of MPs to adequately meet 
growing local demands relating to rural in frastructure, drinking water, education, 
health facilities and community assets. At the same time, the cost of construction 
materials, labour and infrastructure deve lopment has increased substantially due to

allocation from Rs. 5 crore to at least Rs. 10 crore per Member of Parliament. Such an

Concern over the incident of adulterated milk in Rajamahendravaram,   
Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI SUBHAS CHANDRA BOSE PILLI (Andhra Pradesh): In late February 2026, the 
residents in localities such as Swar oop Nagar and Chowdeswari Nagar in 
Rajahmundry, Andhra Pradesh,  fell ill with symptoms like vomiting, abdominal pain 
and acute kidney function (failure to produce urine) after consuming milk supplied by 
local dairy vendor. Samples of milk and c linical specimens were sent to labs for 
forensic and chemical analysis.  Many pe ople died after consuming the suspected 
milk with death toll rising to 8 to 9 as pe r the official updates. 20-25 persons were 
hospitalized who are threatened with kidn ey complications requiring dialysis and 
ventilator support and are in critical condition. The Food Safety and Standards 
Authority of India (FSSAI) sought a detailed report and is monitoring the case closely 
with Andhra Pradesh State Government. The contaminated milk was traced back to a 
local diary unit in Narasapuram Village, Ko rukonda Mandal, East Godavari District. 
The Government and officials have issued a detailed public Health Bulletin on the 
incident, confirming that many people we re diagnosed with symptoms like severe 
kidney stress, high blood urea and high cr eatinine levels and these are the symptoms 
of kidney failure. I urge the Central Gove rnment to order a detailed enquiry in the 
matter. I also urge the Government to pr ovide financial assistance to the affected 
families. Thank you, Sir.

FAREWELL TO THE RETIRING MEMBER 
MR. CHAIRMAN:  Honourable Members, today, we bid farewell to our esteemed 
colleague, Shri Ranjan Gogai , nominated Member of this house, who is retiring 
today, that is, 16th of March, 2026, on completion of his term of office.  
S
hri Ranjan Gogai, former Chief Justice of India, began his association with the 
august in March, 2020, following his nomination by the honourable President of India. 
As a distinguished jurist, he brought unparalleled legal acumen and experience to the 
deliberations of the Rajya Sabha. His intervention in the Rajya Sabha reflected his 
deep understanding of legislative processes and public interest. The House will, 
certainly, miss his wise counsel, measured intervention and the gravitas he brought to 
our discussions. I wish that he will continue to contribute to the nation in different 
capacities with the same dedication, integrity and the spirit of service that he has 
exemplified throughout his illustrious career.  
On behalf of the entire House, I extend my best wishes to Shri Ranjan Gogai 
for good health, happiness and many more years of fruitful service to the nation.

Demand to establish an AIIMS at Raichur in Karnataka 
SHRIMATI SUDHA MURTY (Nominated): I am standing here today on behalf of the 
peo
ple of Karnataka, especially on behalf of the people of Kalyana Karnataka (North 
Karnataka), to make a request to the Central Government. Our Central Government 
has established All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in many states, but 
there is none in Karnataka. For this reason, I request the honourable Government to 
please consider our Karnataka. I am not asking for this hospital for Hubballi or 
Bengaluru; I am asking for Raichur district. Raichur district is very backward. 
According to NITI Aayog, it is one of the many backward regions. By the grace of the 
kings of the Kingdom of Mysore, South Karnataka has grown to be prosperous. But, 
in the last 250 years, under the rule of others, North Karnataka has been neglected or 
forgotten. There are no proper healthcare facilities there. There is extreme poverty, 
health issues and a lack of education. Even if there are institutions, they are not of 
high quality. It is because of this, the poor people there spend more on their 
healthcare than those living in Bengaluru or other large areas. If they have any health 
problems, they have to travel to distant Bengaluru or Hyderabad. In such a situation,

Demand for preservation of old Koirengei Airfield of Manipur as part of  
India's national heritage 
SHRI MAHARAJA SANAJAOBA LEISHEMBA (Manipur):  Thank you, Sir. My Zero 
Hour mention is -‘Demand for preservation of old Koirengei airfield of Manipur as part 
of India's national heritage’. Sir, I draw the kind attention of the Government 
regarding the historical significance of the old Koirengei airfield of Manipur and urgent 
need for its preservation as part of India's national heritage. It was constructed during 
1942-43 with the assistance of American engineers. This airfield played a crucial role 
in the Allied Defence during the Battle of Imphal in World War-II. It served as a key 
supply and support base for the Allied Forces and played an important role to stop 
Japanese advance into India.  
Earlier, in 1942, when Japanese forces advanced into Burma, the Imphal valley 
became a major route for the evacuation of civilians. This airfield served as an 
important humanitarian corridor where displaced families, children and the sick 
received food, shelter and medical assistance. This airfield supported the vital air-
bridge that sustained nearly 2,00,000 Allied troops and helped secure India’s Eastern 
frontier. It was the last departure point of Major General Orde Wingate and later 
served as the landing ground where India’s first Prime Minister, Nehru ji, was formally 
welcomed in Manipur.                                                   
 However, the physical remains of this airfield are gradually disappearing due to 
unregulated constructions and military presence. People of Manipur are also very 
disappointed to see the deteriorating condition of the airfield. Preserving this site will 
protect its historical legacy and will enable future generations to understand India’s 
wartime resilience and humanitarian commitment. I, therefore, urge the Government 
to take up necessary steps, in coordination with the Ministry concerned and the State 
Government, to preserve and protect the historical ‘Old Koirengei Airfield’ as a 
National Heritage Airfield Site. Thank you, Sir.

Demand for legislation on withdrawal and withholding of life-sustaining  
medical treatment for terminally-ill patients 
SHRI HARISH BEERAN (Kerala):  Thank you, Chairman, Sir, for giving me this 
opportunity. Sir, I want to draw the attention of the House to a very serious matter.  
Last week, the Supreme Court had delivered a judgement by which it allowed the 
withdrawal of life support system to a terminally-ill patient. Shri Harish Rana, a healthy 
young man, who had an accidental fall in 2013 from the fourth floor of his paying guest 
accommodation, was in coma for the entire 13 years. He was in permanent vegetative 
state, 100 per cent disabled and was on clinically assisted nutrition and hydration. His 
parents did not have any other option but to move the Court. I spoke to their lawyer, 
Rashmi Nandakumar, a friend of mine, who told me that the resilience shown by the 
family during this entire personal trauma was commendable.  
 Sir, while delivering the judgement, the Supreme Court Judges, Justice 
Jamshed Pardiwala and Justice K. V.  Viswanathan, with tears in their eyes, told the 
parents that  “You are not giving  up on your son,  you are allowing him to leave with 
dignity.” The Supreme Court also realised that they are stepping into an arena where 
there is no legislation.  Article 21 of the Constitution says that there is a Right to Life 
14
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
with dignity. That has been stretched to Right to Die with dignity. But, how much 
mor
e can the Supreme Court stretch is the question? My issue, Sir, is that there is no 
legislation despite all these things. In 2006, 196 th Law Commission Report 
com
prehensively examined the issue of passive euthanasia, appended a draft law, 
but Parliament did nothing. In 2011, the Supreme Court was forced to step in Aruna 
Shanbaug’s case and framed guidelines because the Parliament did nothing. In 2012, 
241st Report of the Law Commission, again, had a draft law, but the Parliament did 
noth
ing.  In 2018, the Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in Common Cause 
case issued elaborate guidelines noting that they will operate only till the Parliament 
framed a law, but the Parliament did nothing. In 2023, the Supreme Court modified its 
guidelines till the time the Parliament enacts a law, the Parliament did nothing.   In 
2026, the latest judgement of the Supreme Court also expresses the hope that 
Parliament legislates on the subject. 
 Sir, we talk endlessly about protecting the poor from financial distress. Over 65 
per cent of all healthcare expenditure in our country is paid entirely out-of-pocket by 
the families. Yet, we refuse to pass a law. Sir, no doctor or a healthcare professional 
will be prepared to take the risk. Also, Sir, there are similar legislations in the foreign 
countries, but we are not prepared.    
 Sir, my State Kerala has shown the nation what dignified end of life looks like.  
Since 2008, Kerala has been running a community-based palliative care programme,   
reaching every Gram Panchayat, integrating 500 NGOs. Sir, I urge the Government to 
introduce a medical treatment of terminally-ill patients (end of life) bill as 
recommended by the Law Commission and to mandate  palliative care infrastructure 
at every district hospital and  Primary Healthcare Centres. Honourable Nadda ji is 
there.  I commend to him, Sir.  Thank you.

Demand for stringent laws to prevent disruptions during international  
events in India 
SHRI JAGGESH (Karnataka): Sir, I wish to raise a matter concerning India's global 
reputation as a reliable host for international events. Firstly, I congratulate the 
Government of India, under the leadership of Shri Narendra Modi, for successfully 
organizing the AI Impact Summit, 2026 in Delhi. The event brought together global 
18
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
leaders, inventors and experts in artificial intelligence and highlighted India's growing 
strength in technology. Innovation enhanced India's global image and increased 
opportunities for investment, partnerships and knowledge sharing. However, I 
strongly condemn the disruptive and irresponsible action by members of Congress 
Party during the Summit. Attempting to disturb such an important international event 
is completely unacceptable and reflects poorly on the country. Such action risks 
public safety and can damage India's reputation before the global community. 
Sir, the Modi Government is working hard to manage the impact of global 
conflicts and ensure stable LPG supplies. But it is unbecoming of a grand old party 
like the Congress Party to spread panic about LPG supply for political advantage 
during a national challenge. It takes many years to build a nation's image, but a single 
careless act can harm it. The nation and its reputation must always come before any 
party or individual. In international platforms, it is India that is represented before the 
world and, therefore, everyone must act with responsibility and keep the national 
interest of our political benefits. I urge the Government to treat this matter with utmost 
seriousness and enact clear and stringent laws to deal with any disruptive actions by 
individuals, groups or political parties during international events held in India. Such 
measures are essential to safeguard public order, protect India's global reputation 
and ensure that such incidents never repeat. Thank you, Sir.

Pilot fatigue and FDTL rules 
*241.    SHRI SAKET GOKHALE: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to 
state: 
(a)  the reasons for granting temporary exemptions to certain airlines from the 
new Flight Duty Time Limitations (FDTL) rules until February 2026; 
(b)  whether the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has conducted a 
safety risk assessment before allowing these exemptions; and 
(c)  the number of fatigue-related safety occurrences reported by pilots during 
this exemption period till date? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI KINJARAPU RAMMOHAN NAIDU):  (a) to 
(c) A statement is laid on the table of house. 
Statement 
 (a) The 'temporary exemptions' were granted to various airlines from the new 
Flight Duty Time Limitation (FDTL) regulations under CAR Section 7 Series J Part III 
based on operational constraints as submitted by the airlines, subject to review after a 
period of six months from the date of implementation, i.e., 01.11.2025. 
 Further, IndiGo was granted a one-time temporary exemption from two 
clauses of the FDTL regulations, valid from 05.12.2025 to 10.02.2026, in order to 
stabilize the disruptions experienced in December 2025 and to reduce passenger 
inconvenience. 
 (b) Safety Risk Assessment (SRA) is submitted by the airlines and is duly 
examined by DGCA before granting any variation. 
 (c) No fatigue-related safety occurrences have been reported by pilots during 
this exemption period till date.

Ground inspection of JMM works 
*
242.  SHRI PRAMOD TIWARI: Will the Minister of JAL SHAKTI be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of households provided access to potable tap water 
connections since 2022 under Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) and the 
percentage it constitutes of rural population; 
(b) whether the JMM in the past has been marred with irregularities; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government for ground inspection of the JMM works? 
THE MINISTER OF JAL SHAKTI (SHRI C R PATIL): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on 
the table of the House. 
Statement 
 (a) Since August 2019, Government of India is implementing Jal Jeevan 
Mission (JJM) – Har Ghar Jal, in partnership with States/ UTs, to make provision of 
safe and adequate tap water connection to every rural household of the country. As 
reported by States/UTs on JJM IMIS, more than 8.53 crore rural households have 
been provided with tap water connections since financial year 2021-22, which 
constitutes about 44% of the total rural households in the country. Thus, as on date 
the overall coverage of rural households with tap water connections has increased 
from 3.23 crore (16.72%) in 2019 to 15.82 crore (81.74%). 
  (b) and (c) As per the data reported by all States/ UTs, a total of 18,790 
complaints have been received by States/ UTs from different sources such as media 
reports, suo-moto cognizance, references from public representatives, citizens, 
grievance portal, etc. regarding financial irregularities and poor quality of works under 
JJM. States/ UTs have also reported that action has been taken against 635 
Departmental Officials, 1,020 contractors, and 155 Third Party Inspection Agencies 
(TPIAs). The State-wise details of complaints received and action taken against 
officials, contractors and third-party agencies are annexed.  
  Furthermore, States/ UTs have been repeatedly advised to adopt a zero-
tolerance approach toward any financial, procedural, or quality-related violations. All 
States/ UTs have been advised to ensure that every complaint is duly examined, field 
verification is carried out promptly and all required disciplinary, contractual, and legal

  (d)  To ensure the successful implementation of JJM, Government of India 
has been regularly reviewing the implementation with respective State Governments 
through review meetings and visits of multi-disciplinary teams to highlight the areas to 
strengthen implementation and monitoring of the mission. Further, several initiatives 
have been undertaken to strengthen the monitoring mechanism under JJM through 
ground inspection of water supply schemes, are as under:  
(i) States have been conducting monthly inspections of four schemes each, 
assigned by the Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS), to 
strengthen field-level oversight. State-level teams inspect the schemes to 
assess the quality of construction, adherence to timelines, availability of 
services, and resolution of issues and submit their reports on JJM –IMIS. 
(ii) Central Nodal Officers were appointed by Government of India for ground 
truthing of JJM schemes and the reports submitted by them have been shared 
with States/ UTs for necessary corrective measures.  
(iii) Ground verification has been enhanced by strengthening the monitoring 
framework for National WASH Experts (NWEs) through a revised and 
comprehensive checklist emphasizing quality of execution, along with a revised 
Terms of Reference (ToR) for TPIs to ensure effective supervision.  
(iv) Central Prabhari Officers (CPOs) for Aspirational Blocks and Aspirational 
districts have also been sensitized to review rural piped water supply schemes 
under JJM during their field visits and have been provided with a digital 
reporting mechanism. 
(v) Under Jal Seva Adhyan, a recent initiative of Department of Drinking Water and 
Sanitation, in collaboration with All India Council of Technical Evaluation, 
engineering students under the guidance of technical mentors have undertaken 
assessment of piped water supply schemes and share their observations with 
the Department. 
(vi) Jal Seva Aankalan is a digital tool enabling community-led self-review process 
and ground verification process, through which villages assess the 
performance of their piped water supply systems on parameters such as

MR. CHAIRMAN:  Q. No. 243.   
Installation of advanced weather forecasting and air traffic management systems 
*243.    SHRIMATI SULATA DEO : Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to 
state: 
42
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
(a)  whether Government proposes to install advanced weather forecasting and 
air 
traffic management systems at airports in cyclone-prone coastal area in 
the State of Odisha; and 
(b)  if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI KINJARAPU RAMMOHAN NAIDU):  (a) 
and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
 (a) and (b) Continuous efforts are being taken by the Government of India to 
improve the meteorological infrastructure in Odisha, including the Installation of 
advanced weather observations, monitoring and forecasting system at airports in 
cyclone - prone coastal Odisha. Currently, Odisha has a total of five operational 
airports. All these airports have been supported with advance current weather 
monitoring Instruments. Further, the airport at Bhubaneswar is supported with latest 
Integrated Aviation weather automatic stations and Runway Visibility Reporting 
(RVRs) systems for helping flights to land during bad weather owing to Cyclone, 
heavy rains, low clouds, poor visibility etc. The State has also been equipped with 
state of art Doppler Weather Radar (DWRs) networks with 2 DWR installed at Paradip 
and Gopalpur especially to help in monitoring and tracking Cyclones and provide 
advance warning over the airports. 
 A Cyclone Warning Centre (CWC) is functional in IMD, Bhubaneswar to 
support all aviation related operations for the State during the cyclone period. All 
aviation related bulletins and warnings including cyclone warning, Aerodrome 
Forecasts and airfield warnings (local) and area forecast are provided by IMD, 
Bhubaneswar. 
 Further, a new Air Traffic Management (ATM) Automation System has been 
commissioned at Bhubaneswar Airport on 06.02.2024 by the Airports Authority of 
India.

SHRI KINJARAPU RAMMOHAN NAIDU: Sir, the honourable Member has asked about 
the impact of cyclones on civil aviation operations, especially in coastal areas. I truly 
understand the seriousness with which she has put the question because I also come 
from Srikakulam, which is right adjacent to Odisha and is also a coastal area. The 
cyclones that have been mentioned, be it 1999 cyclone or Hudhud or Phailin, all these

operations, the weather data or the meteorological data is provided by the IMD, 
which is a different department. Taking the data that has been provided by them, 
aircraft operations are carried out in a very safe and secure manner. Regarding the 
infrastructure that has been set up in Odisha for getting better weather-related 
information, Integrated Aviation Weather Automatic Stations and Runway Visibility 
Reporting Systems have been set up at Bhubaneswar airport, which is the 
international and biggest airport in Odisha. The State has also been equipped with 
state-of-the-art Doppler Weather Radars. Two DWRs have been installed at 
Paradeep and Gopalpur. These are both coastal locations and they provide us with 
data on how the cyclones are coming; the tracking and monitoring of cyclones 
happens through these DWRs. And, two DWRs have already been mentioned. A 
Cyclone Warning Centre (CWC) is also functional in IMD Bhubaneswar, which also 
supports weather-related data. All this data is compiled by IMD and provided to the 
airports, the navigation systems, the aircraft and the pilots, so that their operations 
are not hampered by weather. Thank you.

44.    SHRI KHIRU MAHTO: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state:

Statement 
 (a) to (d) The expansion and upgradation of airports is a continuous process 
and is undertaken by the Airport Operators from time to time, depending on the 
availability of land, commercial viability, socio-economic considerations, traffic 
demand/willingness of airlines to operate to/from such airports. The Airports 
Authority of India (AAI) has undertaken construction of a Parallel Taxi Track (PTT), 
Rapid Exit Track (RET) and reconfiguration of the existing Terminal Building to 
augment the capacity of Ranchi Airport. The timeline for completion of the airport 
projects depends upon many factors, such as land acquisition, availability of 
mandatory clearances, financial closure, etc. 
 Bokaro Airport, owned by Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL), has been 
identified for development under the Regional Connectivity Scheme - 
UdeDeshkaAamNagrik (RCS-UDAN). An amount of Rs. 78.50 crore has been 
incurred towards the development of the airport infrastructure.

THE MINISTER OF JAL SHAKTI (SHRI C R PATIL): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on 
the table of the House. 
Statement 
 (a) to (d) The Government of India is driving a comprehensive transformation 
of the nation’s water landscape through its flagship initiative, the Jal Jeevan Mission 
(JJM) – Har Ghar Jal. Since August 2019, Government of India, in partnership with 
States, is implementing Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM)-Har Ghar Jal to enable every rural 
household in the country, to have assured potable water through tap connection.  
 Water being a State subject, the responsibility of planning, approval, 
implementation, operation, and maintenance of drinking water supply schemes/ 
works, including those under the Jal Jeevan Mission, lies with State/UT 
Governments. The Government of India supports the States by providing technical 
and financial assistance only. If any cases of Google images being used for survey or 
any such deviations from procedure are reported, necessary action is taken by States 
as per extant rules. 
 Further, to enhance transparency and to ensure technically sound 
implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission and also to ensure ground truthing of assets, 
the Sujalam Bharat database is a digital platform designed for  States/UTs to 
systematically map, geotag, and monitor rural water supply assets. It enablesfield-
level data capture and validation for  bulk water , out-village, and  in-
village components, generating unique  Sujal Gaon IDs . As a foundational Digital 
Public Infrastructure (DPI),  it creates a GIS-based digital asset registry, linking 
infrastructure components to ensure a seamless, transparent, and data-driven supply 
chain from source to household. 
 As per the Operational Guidelines of ‘Jal Jeevan Mission’, it is the responsibility 
of National Jal Jeevan Mission (NJJM) to carry out regular functionality assessment, 
evaluation and impact assessment. For the purpose, NJJM selects a 3rd party 
agency through open tendering. In such assessment(s), State/ UTs are given a 
52
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
functionality score on the basis of functionality of samples on quantity (55lpcd or 
mor
e), quality and regularity i.e. water supply to rural households for all 12 months in 
a year or on daily basis. All these parameters are taken to define the functionality of 
the HH tap water connections, as per specified criteria. 
 Since starting of the mission in August 2019, three functionality assessment 
survey has been conducted in 2020- 21, 2021-22 and 2024-25. The reports of the last 
functionality assessment 2024 is also available in public domain at following URL: 
https://jaljeevanmission.gov.in/functionality-report-2024 
 To ensure  regular, adequate, and quality  rural water supply, the Department 
launched "Jal Seva Aankalan " on 30 December 2025. Under this initiative, the  Village 
Water and Sanitation Committee (VWSC) conducts village-level assessments. 
Following a Gram Sabha presentation, the Panchayat Secretary digitally submits the 
data on the  JJM-IMIS Dashboard  for ‘Har Ghar Jal’ villages. District and State 
authorities then review this information to identify service gaps and formulate 
effective improvement plans for sustainable water management.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (DR. DINESH SHARMA):  Now, Shri Saket Gokhale - not 
present. Shri P. Wilson. 
SHRI P. WILSON (Tamil Nadu):  Sir, the Appropriation Bill, 2026, authorises the 
Union Government to withdraw an additional two lakh eighty-one thousand two 
hundred eighty-nine crore and twenty-six lakh (Rs. 281,289,26,00,000) rupees from 
the Consolidated Fund of India for the Financial Year 2025-26. Through this 
legislation, the Government is seeking parliamentary approval to appropriate 
massive additional expenditure for 101 items, mentioned in the Schedule to the Bill, 
to various Ministries and Departments. The Schedule to the Bill lists significant 
allocations, including Rs.19,230 crore for the Department of Fertilizers, Rs.23,641 
crore for the Department of Food and Public Distribution, Rs.17,647 crore for the 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and several other large sums across 
Departments. My question is : why have more funds to the Food and Public 
Distribution Department not been allotted in view of the LPG scarcity? Another 
problem, which we see, as parliamentarians, whenever the Demands for Grants 
come before us, is that the funds are allocated but the funds are not fully utilised by 
the Departments, and there is no action taken against these Departments which do 
not utilise the funds fully.   
Sir, I see from these additional grant allocations that there is no additional 
demand, so far as the Ministry of Social Justice is concerned. For the Scheduled 
Caste and Scheduled Tribe scholarships, they do not allocate enough funds for the 
marginalised people and these students from the marginalised sections suffer a lot.   
So far as the Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare is concerned, 
they have allotted very less amount under the additional grant. But have they 
visualised the problem faced by the farmers? In simple terms, the Bill permits the 
[ 16 March, 2026 ]
73

 
Government to dig deeper into the Consolidated Fund of India, the very pool where 
all taxes, revenues, duties, cess collections, borrowings and receipts of the Union 
Government are deposited, and through an Appropriation Bill, the Government 
obtains the authority to withdraw those public resources. Sir, with regard to transfer 
of Rs. 4,04,115 crore to States, let me remind the House of an important fact. The 
Union Government collects 4 per cent as Education Cess from every citizen of India.  
This Cess was introduced specifically to strengthen the education and health sector 
and to support programs, which fulfill the constitutional mandate under Article 21A, 
namely, the Right to Education. The Cess is meant to finance programs like Samagra 
Shiksha Scheme, which supports teachers, salaries, school infrastructure, inclusive 
education for children with disabilities, digital learning, scholarships and universal 
access to quality education. Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, this Cess goes into the 
Consolidated Fund of India, but here is the shocking reality. While the Union 
Government is collecting the Cess from the people of India and putting it into the 
Consolidated Fund of India, it is diverting it through the Appropriation Bill like the one 
which we are discussing here. It is not realizing that the funds are meant for education 
sector in the States like Tamil Nadu. Tamil Nadu alone owes nearly Rs. 3,548 crores 
under this Samagra Shiksha. In its Report of March, 2025, the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Education, which included Members from the Ruling Party also, clearly 
stated that the delay in releasing funds under Samagra Shiksha Scheme by the Union 
Government are unjustifiable and it gave directions to immediately release funds. It 
has been one year since the Report has been submitted, but the Union Government is 
not releasing the funds. The Government continues to sit on these funds and is asking 
for another 2.81 lakh crore of rupees to be appropriated from the Consolidated Fund 
of India. Sir, this is fiscal discrimination. The injustice does not stop here. Several 
crucial Central Schemes funds owed to Tamil Nadu remain pending. According to 
detailed representation made by the Tamil Nadu Government, the Union Government 
owes more than 10,000 crore of rupees across various schemes. Sir, take the 
example of Jal Jeevan Mission. The Union Government has released only Rs. 5,914 
crores leaving Rs. 3,100 crores still pending. Take the example of Hogenakkal 
Combined Water Supply. Here, they have dropped the scheme. When we proposed 
to give Rs. 7,590 crores, they said they will give their share, but, today, that is 
dropped! Sir, what message does it give? When it comes to collecting taxes and 
revenues from Tamil Nadu, the Union Government shows no hesitation but when it 
comes to returning funds meant for the welfare schemes, suddenly, the Centre 
develops financial constraints!

[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, even under MGNREGA, which supports the poor rural 
hou
seholds, we have Rs. 729.88 crores as pending liabilities for Tamil Nadu, delaying 
wage payments to workers. Under the Finance Commission’s grants for the local 
bodies and disaster preparedness, another Rs. 2,246 crore remain unpaid. In spite of 
all this, the Union Government is asking Parliament to approve another Rs. 2.81 lakh 
crore appropriation from the Consolidated Fund of India. This is nothing but selective 
fiscal governance.   
Sir, I rise to draw the deepening crisis in India's textile sector caused by the 
Government's complete failure to defend our industry against hostile global trade 
developments. India's textile and apparel sector employs more than 45 million 
workers, contributing 2 per cent to the national GDP, 13 per cent to industrial 
production and 12 per cent to India's total exports. Yet, today, this vital sector is 
under severe distress because the Government has failed to protect it from the 
international developments. With the new US-Bangladesh agreement, Bangladeshi 
manufacturers are shifting towards US cotton, putting at risk the Indian cotton and 
yarn exports worth 600 to 650 million US dollars. This is not merely a trade 
adjustment. It is a direct blow to Indian cotton farmers and spinning mills.  The crisis 
has already devastated major textile clusters. In Tamil Nadu, Tirupur is one of India's 
largest knitwear hubs. Exports fell by 37 per cent in 2025, leading to loss of 2 lakh 
jobs. Factories are shutting down; orders are being cancelled and workers are being 
forced to migrate in search of another livelihood. If urgent action is not taken, 
including reducing the tariff imposed by the US, securing tariff parity in global 
markets, removing the cotton import duty and protecting exporters from unfair trade 
practices, India risks losing a sector that sustains millions of livelihoods.                                                                 
3.00 P.M. 
 Sir, now let me talk about the crisis that reflects the Government’s policy 
failure, the LPG situation in the country. The food distribution department is not 
allocated with enough funds. In 2011, when LPG prices were raised by Rs. 50, leaders 
of the present ruling party marched on the streets carrying cylinders and accusing the 
Government of being anti-people and asked where aam admi ki Government is, that 
is, people’s Government. In 2014, when this Government came to power, global 
crude oil prices were roughly in the same range as we see them today. Even today, 
crude oil prices largely hover around 70 dollars to 100 dollars per barrel, which is not 
dramatically different from the global price environment that existed earlier. Yet, 
despite similar crude price levels, the price of the domestic LPG cylinder is almost 
[ 16 March, 2026 ]
75

 
double. So, I wanted to ask this Government: Where is a am aadmi ki Government 
that once you promised? When the global crude prices are almost comparable, why 
has the burden on ordinary households increased so drastically? Instead, the burden 
has increased because of the taxation policies and pricing mechanism imposed by the 
Union Government. India consumes about 80,000 tons of LPG per day, roughly 30 to 
31 million tons annually. But our national storage capacity barely covers three to four 
weeks of consumption and strategic reserves are extremely limited. Nearly 60 to 67 
per cent of our LPG is imported mostly from West Asia through the Strait of Hormuz, 
marking India highly vulnerable to geopolitical disruption. Instead of building strategic 
reserves and strengthening supply chains, the Government has allowed supply 
uncertainty and price escalation. Energy experts and policy analysts have been 
warning for years that India's heavy dependence on imported LPG leaves the country 
extremely vulnerable to global disruption. Any geopolitical tension, regional conflict, 
war or blockade in major energy corridors can immediately affect supply chains and 
availability. Today those warnings have become a reality. The consequences are 
severe. In Tamil Nadu alone, over 60,000 factories and commercial establishments 
depend on LPG and similar fuels. Small eateries, hotels and food businesses are 
struggling because of cost surge and erratic supply. While the Union Government has 
failed to act, the Tamil Nadu Government, under the honourable Chief Minister, Mr. 
M.K. Stalin, has stepped forward to protect its people. The State Government has 
introduced electricity subsidies at rupees two per unit for eateries shifting to induction 
cooking. It has provided concessional loans for MSMEs to adopt electric cooking 
equipment. But, Sir, a serious question arises. Across several States, particularly 
those heading to elections, LPG supply appears to be selectively managed, creating 
artificial demand pressures and public dissatisfaction.  If the Government believes that 
political manipulation of essential commodities will help it win elections, it is gravely 
mistaken. The people of Tamil Nadu are politically conscious and socially aware.  
They know who collects the taxes; they know who withholds their funds; they know 
who stands with them in time of crisis.  I would like to quote a Thirukural. and“T he 
world will constantly embrace the feet of the great King who rules over his subjects 
with love. A just king who cherishes his people will have a world that stands by his 
side.” This kural tells us that when a ruler governs by embracing and protecting his 
people, the world itself will stand in the loyalty at its feet. ( Time-bell rings) One 
minute, Sir.  The leader who stands with his people in difficult times earns not just 
authority but the enduring trust of the people.

SHRIMATI SUDHA MURTY (Nominated):  Sir, normal grants are given during the 
Budget, but you cannot run a nation of 1.4 billion people with a rigid Budget.  It 
requires extra money intermittently and that is the reason our Constitution allows it 
three times in a year. First installment was given in the Winter Session. Now, this is 
due in this Session. SDGF does not run on strict rules. Depending on the ground 
reality, it changes. Being a neutral person, I want to tell this one. Everybody talks that 
gas cylinder price is up. I understand the difficulties of our honourable Petroleum 
Minister. We never started the war. We never asked for rise in gas price. We never 
asked for petrol price rise. It is the whole world which is affected; it is not just India. 
[ 16 March, 2026 ]

d
amaged in Iran, we cannot repair it. Please understand it. None of you here, I think, 
in this august gathering, have seen 1962 war. When I was a 10 or 12 years old girl, we 
have undergone what a war means, what sacrifice has to be made in the war and you 
have to adjust!  So, I request everyone to understand the situation. It is not that we 
started this; someone started this and the whole world suffers. 
 In the second Supplementary Demand, it is Rs. 2.81 lakhs crores. Out of that, 
Rs. 0.80 lakhs will be either by recovery or savings from Ministries. So, ultimately, we 
are going to raise almost approximately Rs. 2.8 lakh crore. Running a Budget is like 
running a house. Being a housewife, I know the importance of rainy days, which I 
exercised in my own life, where I saved money without anybody's knowledge and it 
helped and changed my life. Similarly, I congratulate this Government. They have 
started ESF, that is, Economic Stabilisation Fund. That means, for the rainy days, we 
have to save a certain amount of money, which will help. That is Rs. 57,000 crores.  
Unpredictable difficulties have come in our country or, sometimes, even in the world 
for that matter. In 2019-20, it was the COVID era, so we had to undergo difficult time. 
In 2022, it was the Russian-Ukraine war. In 2023, it was Hamas conflict. In 2025, it 
was complex tariff problem. In 2026, it is the West Asia problem. Tell me, when you 
have everyday problem, is it not wise to save some money? So, Rs. 57,000 crores is 
taken from this. We are left with Rs. 1.43 lakh crore in the Supplementary Demand. I 
congratulate the Government starting this very good scheme of ESF. Chanakya or 
Kautilya’s Arthashastra says, ‘What is a prosperous country? A country which has a 
robust defence is a prosperous country’. He gives Saptanga. One of them I am telling 
you. One of them is that you should have an excellent defence system. We have seen 
what has happened in the Operation Sindoor. So, you are giving Rs. 41,000 crores 
approximately to Defence, which is very, very essential. They look after us; our 
soldiers look after us, so that we can live in a democratic India. We should be ever 
grateful to our Armed Force or all three Forces for that matter. So, out of this, money 
is used actually for salary, pension, health and many other issues because they are 
essential. You cannot compromise in that and Rs. 6,100 crores goes to Ex-
Servicemen Contributing Health Scheme.  I have a request to the Government. I may 
suggest a small change for this. We should reconsider change in tax status for 
disability pension for those service people who have attained superannuation because 
they have given a part of their body to our country. So, this is my request to the 
Finance Ministry. In Raghuvansham, Kalidasa describes, through Raja Dilipa, what

the lifeline of our country and we do not want to keep him or her in the second

and other things, 90 per cent of them are imported. And, in today's scenario, it is not

 The third one is PM Garib Kalyan Yojana. I have to tell two more things about

this. This is the most important thing because nobody should go hungry with the 
rising prices because of the West Asia’s conflict. We have to take care of the people.

process, they have given Rs. 23,000 crore. When you deduct all these things, the

I feel this is a very good Bill and it is very appropriate to give importance to 
Defence, importance to farmers and we are making a new Fund of Rs. 57,000 crore.  
So, I consider this Bill as well designed, appropriation is very nice and I support this

trade, and our country is trying to do all those things. When you do these things, we

SHRI NIRANJAN BISHI (Odisha): “M r. Vice- Chairman, Sir, the Parliament 
authorizes our Government of India to spend money from the Consolidated Fund of 
India for developmental works like education, health, agriculture, and various other 
development projects. This is fine, Sir. However, in our country, 1.5 crore tribal 
people have been displaced and marginalized due to various development projects, 
such as mines, industry, wildlife sanctuaries, national parks, power plants, and 
national highways—especially the tribals of Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, and 
Andhra Pradesh. They are not being properly rehabilitated or resettled. Funds should 
be allotted for that. In the Sardar Sarovar Dam, 85,000 tribals were displaced; in the 
Polavaram Dam project, 300 tribal villages are being displaced. They should be 
resettled suitably. Sir, in our State, Odisha, 5,632 government schools have been 
closed in tribal villages and rural areas; funds should be allotted for the reopening of 
those schools. In our Anwesha Hostels, where ST/SC students used to study, 
admissions have been closed for the last two years. The Government of India should 
allot funds so that ST/SC students can study in private English medium schools. 
Also, for the ST/SC students who were pursuing GNM and BSc Nursing course, they 
used to receive ₹50,000 per year for their studies, but that has also been stopped. 
The Government should provide stipends and allot funds for these ST/SC children. 
Furthermore, in the NSFDC (National SC/ST Finance and Development 
Corporation), no tribals or SC/ST individuals are receiving any kind of loan, subsidy, 
or concession; funds should be allotted for this. Also, the Government should allot 
funds for the livelihood of our PVTGs (Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups). Under 
TRIFED, the minor forest produces that tribals collect and sell to earn a living are not 
getting any MSP (Minimum Support Price), no input subsidies, and there are no 
market facilities. Therefore, the lives of the 15 crore tribals in India have become 
miserable.  It was Baba Saheb Ambedkar's dream to bring the ST/SC people, who 
are at the last rung of India's ladder and are neglected, into the mainstream of the 
country. These ST/SCs are a neglected, exploited, oppressed, and toiling mass; the 
"Voice of the Voiceless" for these tribal and Dalit brothers must be heard. Whether it 
is the Consolidated Fund, the TSP (Tribal Sub-Plan), or the SCSP (Scheduled Caste

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (DR. DINESH SHARMA): The next speaker is Shri S Niranjan 
Reddy; twelve minutes.  
SHRI S NIRANJAN REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, while this is a 
recurring feature in relation to the Supplementary Demands for Grants, there are two 
issues that keep coming every year. I want to focus on these two issues which are 
food and fertilizer. The third issue I want to speak about today would be on transfers 
to States. On the first issue of food, the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and 
Public Distribution seeks an additional Rs. 23,641.28 crores under the Pradhan Mantri 
Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana. This is important. This needs to be sanctioned. But, I have 
a few concerns. It is not just about this Supplementary Demand in relation to this 
amount for this year. As of January 2026, as we speak, the foodgrain stocks in India 
are 59.45 million tonnes. The required buffer norm for India's population would be 
21.41 million tonnes. So, we are having much more than the required buffer stocks. I 
would want to elaborate a little to explain how flawed agricultural policies are leading 
to this lopsided development of certain cropping patterns and mono-cropping 
patterns in India. When we carry foodgrain stocks of 59.45 million tonnes, and when 
India is required to hold 21.41 million tonnes, undisputably, this means that we have 
to carry additional, substantial carrying and storage cost. We need godowns and we 
need to ensure that foodgrains are stored properly so that they do not spoil. So, this 
additional carrying and storage cost is all money that is going waste.  It is because, 
we have the Minimum Support Prices to farmers—which is recommendatory—and I 
find, since this Minimum Support Prices are being granted without a lot of 
forethought, this is leading to changing crop patterns and increasing monocropping, 
as I mentioned. So, this is resulting in India producing more wheat and more rice, 
including in States that traditionally have not been rice-growing States. This is 
resulting in India stocking up these buffers while India has been slowly reducing the 
growth of pulses, edible oils and other things.                
 So there is an increasing import bill. On the one hand, we have an increasing 
cost in relation to procuring food grains that we do not need, while on the other hand, 
India is spending more money on importing food and oil items that are needed for 
India. This needs to be attended to by the Government in the longer run; otherwise, 
every year, we will have the supplementary demand for grants in relation to food. 
Usually, the Comptroller and Auditor General applies what is known as the cost-

benefit ratio; if we are spending one rupee from the Indian Government, what is the

enefit that we get? Sir, look at the two crops that I specifically mentioned. There 
may be other crops. I am not too much of an agriculturalist. I am not an expert, there 
are other people who know this more, but I am just focusing onto for explaining the 
symptoms of the problem.  In relation to rice and wheat, we have to factor in first, the 
fertilizer cost and I will be dealing about that in a few minutes. We have to factor in the 
MSP cost, which is higher than the cost that is generally available in the market. 
Third, we have to factor in the energy cost because most State Governments are 
giving free power by subsidizing it, which is not coming in the cost. Fourth, we have 
to factor in environmental cost. We have seen that in States like Punjab, now 
increasingly in Telangana, because people have shifted to growth of rice in huge 
quantities, with huge fertilizers that are being used, it is resulting in water depletion, it 
is resulting in percolation of fertilizers in the ground.  
[THE VICE-CHAIRPERSON (SHRIMATI S. PHANGNON KONYAK) in the Chair.] 
This is going to have a long-term effect on the country's health and our 
environment. In the cost benefit ratio, one way is to factor in the environmental cost.  
The fifth item is the water cost. Madam, I attended a lecture by one agricultural 
scientist, who is a very celebrated member of NITI Aayog formerly. He mentioned that 
for every kg of rice that is produced, we consume 200 kgs. of water. Even if India 
imports one kg of rice--it may be more than 200 kgs, I am being conservative; I do 
not want to err--if India is stocking 30 million metric tons of rice, we need to 
recognize that on each of these kgs. of rice, India has wasted 200 kgs. of fresh water. 
Fresh water is an area that is going to be a great concern in future. If we add the 
storage and carrying cost to this, we will have the cost on one side of producing one 
kg of rice or one kg of wheat which we are storing in our godowns because nobody 
requires it at this particular point of time. It is in excess of the buffer-stock we need. 
What do we do? Madam, I ask myself. What we now do is, we understand that this 
rice is not needed for consumption, this wheat is not needed for consumption, we are 
giving it at a great subsidy for ethanol production. If the procurement price of the 
Central Government is one rupee, at a discount, it is selling this rice for ethanol 
production. Ethanol production is salutary. It helps us improve our self-reliability in 
relation to petroleum and gas products. But we may have to follow what Brazil is 
doing. We may have to grow crops that will help us increase our ethanol rather than 
over-produce two or three items for which we then pay more, suffer environmental 
consequences and because we have no other option, give it to ethanol production.

tilizers because in the supplementary demands, it requires Rs.15,000 crore 
additional allocation under the nutrient-based subsidy. Madam, you will be surprised 
that while India is highly dependent and, this is a known fact, importing 100 per cent 
of potash requirements and 90 per cent of phosphatic raw materials, the 
recommended nitrogen, phosphorous, potassium ratio for Indian soil is 
approximately, 4:2:1. I repeat, Madam, it is 4:2:1. But, in agriculturally intensive States 
such as Punjab and Haryana, the ratio of fertilizer being applied by farmers -- I remind 
everyone the requirement is 4 :2:1, -- comes to 30 :10:1!  We are providing more than 
seven times the required ratio or five times the required ratio because farmers have 
not been properly trained and also because we have not incentivized the farmers. The 
fertilizer subsidy is being given to fertilizer manufacturers.  We are not applying a 
cost-benefit ratio and giving this fertilizer benefit directly to farmers, which is resulting 
in farmers getting fertilizers and using them indiscriminately. This is leading to burden 
our costs and our Budget. Every year, we spend money on fertilizers through 
Supplementary Demands. If we are able to have a five-year or ten-year plan, over a 
period of time, we reduce this cost on food and fertilizer. At this point, it makes good 
politics because nobody wants to say anything against farmers’ interests. I am not 
speaking against farmers’ interests. I am saying, ‘please protect the farmers.’  But, 
while protecting them, if we can save these costs, the resources can instead be used 
by India for education, health, and defence.

transfers to States in relation to panchayats and urban local bodies. I recognize that I

meaningful debate. And, I am being very honest about this Council speaking about 
States’ interests.  Everybody is parroting the party lines. There is absolutely no clarity 
between the Union’s interest and the States’ interests. Both are in national interest. I 
am happy that the Central Government is making allocations to the State 
Governments, for urban local bodies and panchayats, because the Central 
Government recognizes that the States are not making adequate provisions for them.

only concerned about five-year elections. They work to win the election, get past this

plan that needs to be done. I would like to remind the Central Government that this

of giving it out. The statistics show that this is being done in a partisan manner. The 
best way is to please encourage the States to do it and you make allocations.  
Madam, I recognize that maybe the BJP-ruled States are fiscally the best and most 
responsible States. I am not from that party. But, while I say that, I am saying: Please 
incentivize every party, to have a fiscal responsibility by giving more rather than 
looking at electoral benefits and trying to allocate resources. Madam, I have a few 
more points to make. But, I want to be mindful and stay within my time. I am thankful 
for the opportunity granted to me.                                                                          
THE VICE-CHAIRPERSON (SHRIMATI S. PHANGNON KONYAK): Shri Sandosh 
Kumar P. 
SHRI SANDOSH KUMAR P (Kerala):  Madam Vice-Chairman, today, uncertainty 
looms large over the Indian economy due to external shocks, many of which have 
been aggravated by the policies of the BJP Government. The ongoing conflict in the 
West Asia is not a distant political issue for India; it has direct consequences for our 
trade, employment, remittances and energy security. Unfortunately, despite the 
gravity of the situation, the Union Government appears unprepared. Let us 
understand the scale of India’s economic dependence on the Gulf region. India’s total 
trade with the Gulf Cooperation Council countries is around 178 billion US dollars, and 
our exports to these countries are roughly 56–57 billion US dollars annually .                                                          
These exports include agricultural products, food items, textiles, engineering goods 
and pharmaceuticals. These sectors employ millions of workers across rural and 
semi-urban India. If the conflict continues and trade routes are disrupted, these 
exports will decline. This will directly affect farmers, small producers and workers, 
leading to unemployment, particularly in the rural economy. During such times, the 
rural economy earlier had a cushion in the form of MGNREGA, a right-based program 
that provided livelihood security. But, this Government has systematically weakened 
it. The so-called VB-G RAM G framework is still not even notified. And, the 
allocations are already too low to meaningfully deliver the promised 125 days of 
employment. When export opportunities sink and agriculture incomes fall, how 
exactly does the Government intend to protect rural livelihoods?  
106

The second concern relates to remittances. Madam, nearly 9 to 10 million 
Indians work in the Gulf region and India receives over 129 billion U . S. dollars annually 
in remittances--the highest in the world. A significant portion, I mean, roughly 1/3rd to 
nearly 40 per cent, comes from Gulf countries. These remittances sustain millions of 
families and support the economies of several States. If the conflict persists and 
economic activity slows in the Gulf, employment opportunities for Indian workers may 
shrink and remittances may decline. This will have serious consequences for 
households, regional economies and our foreign exchange flows. What contingency 
plans does the Government have to deal with such a situation? How will it support 
returning workers and protect the families that depend on these incomes? Another 
concern is energy security.

Need for nature-based solutions and risk-informed planning to Urban Planners 
SHRI BRIJ LAL (Uttar Pradesh): Madam, my subject is- Need for Nature-Based 
Solutions and Risk-Informed Planning to Urban Planners. In a recent Case Studies 
Compendium released by the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), in 
February 2026, the agency identified a clear link between poor urban planning, land-
use changes, and the severity of recent disasters. Ecological Lessons for Urban 
Planners. The NDMA emphasizes a "paradigm shift" from traditional engineering to 
nature-based solutions and risk-informed planning: (i) Mainstreaming Climate Risk: 
[ 16 March, 2026 ]
121

 
Planners must incorporate geological, seismic, and climate risk evaluations into 
te
chnical feasibility studies, rather than relying solely on traditional engineering 
parameters. (ii) Protecting Natural Infrastructure: Cities are advised to restore urban 
wetlands, protect floodplains, and create green buffers to manage runoff naturally. 
(iii) Permeable Surfaces: Using permeable and rainwater harvesting is highlighted as 
a cost-effective way to reduce urban flood peaks, which can be 8 times higher in 
developed catchments. (iv) Encroachment Removal: A critical lesson is the urgent 
need to remove encroachments from natural water channels and drains to prevent 
catastrophic urban flooding. If all the above lessons attained from the last 10 recent 
disasters occurred from 2021 to 2024 recommended by NDMA are implemented in 
letter and spirit, we will be able to prevent such disasters in future. I urge the 
Government to look into it. Thank you, Madam.

them. India has nearly 44 crore workers in the unorganised sector, including 
construction workers, domestic workers, street vendors, agricultural labourers, gig 
workers and migrant workers. These workers form the backbone of our economy but 
remain highly vulnerable due to the absence of adequate social security protection. 
The e-Shram portal is an important initiative aimed at registering such workers and 
linking them to welfare measures such as accident insurance, pension schemes and 
other social security benefits. However, despite the progress made so far, a large 
number of workers are not registered on the portal. One of the major reasons is the 
lack of awareness among workers, especially, in rural areas and among migrant 
labourers. Many workers are not aware of the benefits of e-Shram registration or the 
simple procedures involved in enrolling themselves on the portal. As a result, millions 
of eligible workers continue to remain outside the ambit of social security. There is, 
therefore, an urgent need for the Government to conduct aggressive awareness 
campaigns and outreach programmes across the country. Registration camps,

community-level awareness drives, and the involvement of local bodies, trade unions 
a
nd civil society organisations can help ensure that every eligible worker is brought 
under the e-Shram database. I urge the Government to look into it.

Concern over the healthcare services in Kerala due to series of ongoing strikes 
SHRIMATI JEBI MATHER HISHAM (Kerala): Madam, Kerala, a State long celebrated 
for its exemplary healthcare system, is witnessing an unprecedented disruption in 
medical services. With nurses on strike in private hospitals and doctors protesting in 
Government hospitals, the healthcare system is facing a severe standstill. Several 
private hospitals are affected, with thousands of nurses participating in protests 
demanding fair wages and humane working conditions. Surgeries are being 
postponed, admissions restricted, and patients are forced to move from hospital to 
hospital in search of care. At the center of this crisis lies a shocking reality. The basic 
salary of many nurses in private hospitals has remained Rs. 20,000 per month since 
2018. For eight long years, despite inflation, rising costs of living, and the 
extraordinary sacrifices made during the COVID-19 pandemic, these frontline 
healthcare workers have seen virtually no meaningful revision in their wages. If 
Kerala’s hospitals begin to fall silent because its nurses are unheard, the responsibility 
will not lie with the nurses but with the system that ignored them. I urge upon the 
Government to intervene and ensure a fair national framework for nurses’ wages and 
their working conditions.

Concern over adverse impact of India-US trade deal on agricultural interests 
D
R. SYED NASEER HUSSAIN (Karnataka): Madam, there is anxiety in India's 
farming community over the agricultural concessions quietly embedded in the India-
US interim trade deal. Under the deal, India has agreed to eliminate or reduce tariffs 
on all US industrial goods and a wide range of US food and agricultural products, 
including tree nuts, fresh and processed fruit, soybean oil, wine and spirits. India has 
also committed to purchasing 500 billion US dollars of US energy, aircraft, 
technology, and coking coal over the next five years -- an astronomical sum that 
crowds out domestic investment priorities and constrains future budget flexibility. 
Additionally, the situation in the West Asia threatens to further affect the plight of 
farmers, as India imports nearly 40 per cent of its Urea and NPK fertilizers from the 
West Asia, critical for the upcoming Kharif season. Moreover, recently, over 400,000 
tons of Basmati rice were reported stuck at ports due to disruption of trade routes to 
Saudi Arabia and Iran. I urge the Government to look into it.

Concern over town planning recruitment and regulation 
DR. FAUZIA KHAN (Maharashtra):  Madam, there seems to be little concern when 
our cities are planned by those without formal training in the discipline. The effects are 
visible--congested roads, shrinking green spaces, and cities expanding without 
adequate regard for topography or demography. Town planning is a specialized, 
legally recognized discipline, regulated by the UGC and AICTE, and distinct from 
architecture and engineering. Nearly 100 institutions produce around 2,000 qualified 
planners annually. Yet, many State Governments continue recruiting persons without 
planning qualifications to permanent posts, partly because no statutory framework 
exists to guide otherwise. There is also a structural gap worth addressing. Town 
planning is listed under the Twelfth Schedule as a function of Urban Local Bodies; yet 
in practice, it remains with State Governments, whose departments exercise 
significant powers of sanctioning building plans, regulating land use, and preparing 
master plans. The numbers deserve attention. Analysis indicates that in Karnataka, 
only 30 percent of officers are trained planners; in Telangana, 28 per cent; in Kerala, 
32 per cent. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs issued advisories in 2017, 
2019, and 2022, and the NITI Aayog made similar recommendations in 2021. The 
implications are real.  
Public investment in planning education is under-utilized. Cities bearing the 
cost of suboptimal decisions, and qualified professionals unable to contribute where 
they are most needed. A statutory Council for Town and Country Planners,

established by an Act of Parliament, would be a reasonable and necessary step 
f
orward.  I urge the Government to look into it.
