FAREWELL TO THE RETIRING MEMBERS 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon'ble Members, today, we bid farewell to some of our esteemed 
colleagues who would be retiring in the months of April to July this year on completion 
of their term of office. A total of 59 Member s from 20 States will be retiring during this 
period, including 9 women Members. 
Hon'ble Members, our constitutional scheme provides for the retirement of 
one-third of the Members of this House ev ery two years, thereby bringing about a 
periodic change in the composition of this august House. This arrangement ensures 
continuity in the functioning of the Council of States while also creating space for new 
Members to join the House and enrich it s deliberations with their experience and 
insights. This process truly reflects the character of this House as a microcosm of our 
diverse nation. 
26
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
Hon'ble Members, retirement should no t be viewed as an  end, but as the 
beginning of new roles and resp onsibilities. It signifies the passing on of the baton to 
new Members who will carry forward the legacy  of this institution with fresh ideas, 
renewed energy and commitment. At the same time, the experience and wisdom 
gained by the retiring Members during their tenure will continue to guide and inspire 
the next generation of pa rliamentarians. Among the Me mbers retiring are several 
distinguished public figures and veteran par liamentarians who have served the nation 
with dedication for many years in public life. Shriman H. D. Devegowda, former Prime 
Minister of India, is a distinguished leader whose presence has added great stature to 
the House.  With his long experience in pa rliamentary and public life and his deep 
commitment to the interests of farmers and rural communities, he has brought 
valuable perspectives to the debates of th is House.  The House has also benefited 
greatly from the leadership and experience of Shriman Mallikarjun Kharge, the hon. 
Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha.  With his long and distinguished 
parliamentary career in both the Lok Sa bha and the Rajya Sabha, Shriman Kharge 
has been an important voice in the democratic functioning of this House.  I would also 
like to make a particular mention of Shrima n Harivansh, the hon. Deputy Chairman of 
the Rajya Sabha, whose term is also coming to an end on 9 th April 2026.  Shriman 
Harivansh has presided over this House with  dignity, impartiality and a deep sense of 
responsibility. Before entering parliamentar y life, he had a distinguished career in 
journalism and public discourse, and he br ought to this House his vast experience, 
calm demeanour and commitment to parliame ntary traditions. As Deputy Chairman, 
he has guided the proceedings of the Ho use with patience, fairness and wisdom, 
earning the respect and appreciation of Members across the political spectrum.  
Furthermore, he has made meaningful and va luable contributions in several national 
and international parliamentary forums, including the Inter-Parliamentary Union

TRIBUTES TO MARTRYS SARDAR BHAGAT SINGH, RAJGURU AND SUKHDEV 
MR. CHAIRMAN:   Hon.  Members, today, the 23rd of March, marks the anniversary 
of the martyrdom of three of the most valia nt sons of Mother India — Sardar Bhagat 
Singhji, Rajguruji and Sukhdevji — who laid down their lives on this day in 1931 in the 
prime of their youth. Their unparalleled courage, indomitable spirit, and supreme 
sacrifice remain a shining ch apter in our recent struggle for freedom and continue to 
evoke deep respect and gratitude from every citizen of India. 
Hon. Members, their martyrdom was not merely an episode in the history of 
our Freedom Movement, it was a defining moment that awakened the conscience of 
the nation and inspired millions to rise in unity against colonial rule. The freedom that 
we cherish today is the result of the sacr ifice of countless patrio ts and, among them, 
this heroic trio occupies a special place in the heart of every Indian. 
On this solemn occasion, let us reaffirm our resolve to uphold the constitutional 
values and democratic principles for whic h these martyrs stood and to work unitedly 
for a strong, inclusive and progressive India. 
I request the hon. Members to rise in  their places and observe silence as a 
mark of respect to the immortal memory of Sardar Bhagat Singh ji, Rajguru ji and 
Sukhdevji. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.)

Concerns over India’s participation in Pax Silica and its implications for data privacy 
SHRI DIGVIJAYA SINGH (Madhya Pradesh) :  S i r ,  w i t h  y o u r  k i n d  p e r m i s s i o n ,  I  a m  
going to take more than three minutes. I ri se to draw the attention of this august 
House to an important and emerging issue, that is, significance and implications of 
Pax Silica for India’s strategic autonomy, data  privacy and technological sovereignty.  
India has recently joined an international technology coalition known as Pax Silica.   In 
simple terms, Pax Silica is a grouping of co untries aimed at co-operation in standard 
setting in critical areas such as semiconductors, artificial intelligence and digital 
infrastructure, with the dominant role played by the United States.  
 While this initiative may offer certain benefits such as access to secure supply 
chains, increased investments and advance technologies, it also raises serious 
concerns that merit urgent discussion.  The foremost concern relates to data privacy 
and sovereignty.  If India is required to  align and share its standards and systems 
under this coalition, there is a possibilit y that Indian data may be persisted or 
governed through foreign platforms or frameworks.  This raises critical questions 
about the effectiveness and the enforceability of India’s Digital Personal Data 
Protection Act, 2023.  Would the private data of each Indian citizen be protected 
under the DPDP Act?  We want to know th is from the Government.  Secondly, there 
are apprehensions that India’s long-term policy autonomy in such areas as AI 
development, semiconductor strategy and di gital infrastructure may be constrained 
by external standards and over sight.  This could potentially dilute our long-standing 
principle of strategic autonomy and impact  the Government’s stated ‘India First’ 
approach.  In view of these concerns, I urge the Governme nt to clarify (i) the terms 
and conditions of India’s participation in Pax Silica, (ii) the safeguards in place to 
ensure protection and sovereignty of Indian citizens’ data, and (iii) clarify whether this 
arrangement affects India’s inde pendent policy making in criti cal technology sectors.   
This is not merely a technological matter, but one that concerns national security,

Statement 
(a)   Water and Sanitation is State su bject and Management of urban flooding 
falls under the purview of the State Go vernments and the Urban Local Bodies 
(ULBs)/Urban Development Authorities, who are responsible for maintaining the 
drainage and sewerage system. Government of India supplements the efforts of the 
States through schematic interventions/ advisories. It provides financial and technical 
support to the States to strengthen Urban Planning ecosystem.  
Usually, increased incidence of high intensity rainfall in short duration is mainly 
responsible for urban floods, which is fu rther compounded by unplanned growth, 
encroachment of natural water bodies, inadequate sewer systems, inadequate 
rainwater drainage systems, encroachments, etc.   
Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation (A MRUT) launched in 
the year 2015, inter alia, has a component on storm water drainage, which involved 
construction and improvement of drains/ st orm water drains in order to reduce and 
eliminate flooding and creating green space s and parks. Under AMRUT, 838 Storm 
Water Drainage projects worth ₹3017.13 crore have been taken up and 3,798 water 
logging points have been eliminated so far. 
Further, 2,522 green spaces and park projects worth ₹1,604.13 crore have 
been taken up by the States/UTs under AMRUT and 5,286 acres of permeable green 
space area have been developed so far through these projects. 
Under AMRUT 2.0, projects for green sp aces and parks and rejuvenation of 
water bodies are taken up by the States. Under AMRUT 2.0, proposals of the States/ 
UTs for 2,991 water body rejuvenation projects worth ₹6,083.32 crorecovering around 
1,21,800 acres of area and 1,665 gr een spaces and park projects worth ₹1,103.71 
crore covering 13,893.82 acre, have been approved.  
Besides, under AMRUT and AMRUT 2.0 sewerage and septage management 
projects have been undertaken, which inter alia help in evacuation of storm water. 
Under AMRUT, as updated by State/UTs on AMRUT portal, 889 sewerage/septage 
management projects have been grounded, which has led to crea tion of 22,477 km 
length of sewer network. Under AMRUT 2.0, the State/UTs have taken up 584 
Sewerage and Septage Management projects covering 34,559 KM of sewer network.

Concern over protection and dignity of domestic workers 
DR. K. LAXMAN (Uttar Pradesh):   Sir, I draw the attention of Government to the 
condition of domestic workers -- one of the most vulnerable segments of India’s 
unorganized workforce. Domestic workers perform essential services such as 
cleaning, cooking, caregiving, and childcare,  supporting millions of households and 
enabling the functioning of urban economies. According to the E-Shram portal, about 
2.89 crore belong to the domestic and household workers category. A large 
proportion of them is women and migrants  from economically weaker backgrounds. 
Despite their important role, most domestic workers continue to work without written 
contracts, fixed wages, social security coverage or proper grievance redressal 
mechanisms. The Government has taken im portant steps to support unorganized 
workers through initiatives such as the E-Shram portal and the Code on Social

Security, 2020, which aims to extend social security benefits to workers across 
sectors. However, domestic workers face  unique challenges because their work 
takes place inside private homes, making regulation and protection difficult. Many 
remain vulnerable to irregular wages, long working hours, and sudden termination.  
I, therefore, urge the Government to consider recognizing domestic workers as 
‘essential service’ workers and to strengthen their inclusion in welfare programmes 
through better registration, access to so cial security, and effective grievance 
redressal mechanisms.  Such steps will help ensure dignit y, security, and fairness for 
millions of domestic workers as we move toward the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.

(a)  and (b)  Electronics and Information Technology Goods(Requirement of 
Compulsory Registration Order),2021 has been  notified by Ministry of Electronic and 
Information Technology (MeitY) through wh ich Electronics and IT products have 
been brought under compulsory BIS Registrati on as per provisions of Scheme- II of 
BIS (Conformity Assessment) Regulations, 2018. 
Under this Scheme, a licence to use or apply a Standard Mark, through 
registration based on self-declaration of co nformity, is granted for goods or articles, 
hereinafter referred to as products, ma nufactured in a manufacturing premises and 
conforming to all the requirements of the relevant Indian Standard(s). The 
manufacturer ensures that the product has b een tested for conformity against all the 
requirements of the Indian Standard and subm its test report which is issued by third 
party laboratory. 
At present, 65 product categories have been notified under the schedule of 
“Electronics and Information Technology Goods (Requirement of Compulsory 
Registration) Order, 2021 ”. The Order is equally applicable to imported or 
domestically manufactured goods. 
Earlier, as per Scheme-II of Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) Conformity 
Assessment (CA) Regulations, 2018, pr ovisions were available for Central 
Government to notify only Standard(s) fo r compulsory BIS certification. Now vide 
Gazette Notification dated 25th February,  2026 in the BIS Conformity Assessment 
Regulations, 2026, Scheme-II has been am ended to include provisions for Central 
Government to notify essential requir ements also besides Standard (s) for 
compulsory BIS certification.

The ONORC facility has been implemented in all 36 States/Union Territories,

foodgrains from any Fair Price Shop (F PS) across the country using their existing

operates through integration of ration card databases of all States/UTs and 
interoperable ePoS devices at FPSs.

Himalayan terrain.  For over 140 years, it ha s symbolized the region’s cultural identity 
and attracted tourists from India and abroad. However, serious operational and 
maintenance challenges now threaten its survival. Despite efforts by the Ministry of 
Railways, the railway corridor has gradua lly shrunk, compromising safety and 
efficiency. The line passes through land slide prone areas wh ere heavy rainfall 
frequently damages tracks and disrupts services, requiring constant monitoring and 
restoration. Ageing steam locomotives also demand specialised maintenance and 
custom built parts, necessitating sustained technical and financial support. The vision 
of “Vikaas bhi Viraasat bhi ” rightly emphasizes balancing development with heritage 
conservation. This Railway embodies that vision must be preserved through 
sustainable tourism and infrastructure strengthening. There is a need to enhance 
visibility through strategic marketing and to  develop an integrated tourism ecosystem 
linked with local culture and livelihoods. Ac tive participation of local communities, 
tourism stakeholders, and Self Help Groups can generate employment. Skill 
development of youth and railway staff in heritage conservation and modern 
maintenance is equally essential. 
I urge the Government to formulate a comprehensive conservation plan with 
adequate funding, infrastructure restor ation, corridor protection, and disaster 
mitigation measures. Preserving this railway  is preserving a living heritage and the 
identity of the hills.

SHRI MASTHAN RAO YADAV BEEDHA (Andhra Pradesh) : Vice-Chairman Madam, I 
draw attention of the Government to the ur gent need for integrated development of 
the Buckingham Canal corridor in Andhra Prad esh, particularly in Sri Potti Sriramulu 
Nellore District, under National Waterway-4 (NW-4). This calls for coordinated action 
by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Inland Waterways Authority of India 
(IWAI), and convergence with the Sa garmala and Bharatmala programmes. 
Buckingham Canal traverses about 257–258 km  in Andhra Pradesh, and the Nellore 
stretches are less encroached and technically  feasible. Official alignment studies and 
KML-based mapping demarcate a 60-metr e waterway corridor and a 30-metre 
parallel road corridor, safeguarding canal boundaries while enabling planned 
infrastructure development. This allows simultaneous canal restoration and road 
development, unlike congested urban stre tches elsewhere on NW-4. The Nellore 
corridor provides multimodal connectivit y between Krishnapatnam Port and the 
proposed Ramayapatnam Port, linking industrial hubs and hinterland areas. A 
combined road-and-waterway corridor can reduce logistics costs, decongest

industrial cities, generating employment and balanced regional growth. The Union 
Budget 2026–27 reiterates emphasis on in land waterways, port-led development, 
multimodal logistics, and coastal infrastr ucture. The Buckingham Canal corridor is a 
natural candidate for convergence.   I urge upon the Government to sanction a 
Detailed Project Report (DPR), take up the Nellore stretch as a pilot corridor, and 
establish a Centre–State mechanism with IWAI for time-bound execution.

Concern on missing Indian Seafarers in International Waters 
DR. SASMIT PATRA (Odisha): Madam, I seek to highligh t the case of a young cadet 
from Odisha, who has gone missing in in ternational waters under unexplained 
circumstances. At the very beginning of his career, he boarde d a commercial vessel 
with aspirations of supporting his family and building a future. Instead, his sudden 
disappearance, after he was last seen on board has left his family in prolonged 
uncertainty, with no clear answers despite search efforts and limited transparency 
from authorities. This is not an isolated  incident. Official records reveal numerous 
Indian seafarers reported missing or dead under unclear conditions, with many cases 
still pending investigation years later. Thes e include incidents of explosions, onboard 
accidents, disappearances, and even alleged negligence by ship authorities. In one 
case, a cadet went missing mid-voyage  despite multiple onboard searches, 
highlighting serious gaps in monitori ng and accountability. Further, official 
communication indicates that nearly 50 Indian seafarers have died in a single foreign 
region since 2014, many of them between 18 and 24 years old. Several cases also 
point towards mental harassment, unsafe working environments, and delays in 
compensation and investigation. I, therefore, demand time-bound international probe 
into seafarers’ disappearance, mandatory r eal-time tracking and reporting of Indian 
crew on all vessels, a National Maritime Missing Persons Authority and a time-bound 
accountability for all pending cases.

conditions of judges, keeping in mind inte rnational benchmarks and the principle of 
institutional parity.  Strengthening the condit ions of service of judges is ultimately an 
investment in the credibility, independen ce, and effectiveness of India’s justice 
system.

draw the attention of this august Hous e to an important matter concerning the 
ongoing widening and upgradation of NH-66  – the vital corridor connecting Mumbai 
and Goa. This highway serves as the primary road link between the Konkan region of 
Maharashtra and Goa and plays a crucial role  in tourism, trade, transportation of

four-lane highway corridor was sanctioned more than a decade ago with the objective 
of improving connectivity, enhancing road  safety, reducing travel time between

tourists and daily commuters. The completion of this highway will also greatly benefit 
the transportation of goods. Faster and smoother freight movement will support 
industries, agriculture, fisheries and sm all businesses across the Konkan belt and

and economic importance of this highway an d approaching monsoon, it is imperative 
that the project be completed at the earliest on a priority and time-bound basis.

steps to expedite the remaining work on NH-66, ensure better coordination among all 
stakeholders and provide a clear timeline for its early completion, especially before the 
onset of the upcoming monsoon. Thank you.

Concern over commercialization of healthcare and exploitation by  
private hospitals 
SHRI SANT BALBIR SINGH (Punjab) : & Hon’ble Chairman Sir, I thank you for giving 
me this opportunity. Sat Sri Akal to all th e Hon’ble Members present in this House. 
Sir, in our country, doctors have traditionally been accorded the status of God, and 
medical services have always been regard ed as sacred. However, it is deeply 
concerning that healthcare today is increasingly being commercialized and treated as 
a profit-making enterprise. Private hospitals have become prohibitively expensive and 
are beyond the reach of the common man. At the same time, insurance companies 
lure citizens into purchasing policies through tall claims and assurances of 
comprehensive support during medical em ergencies—moments when individuals are 
most vulnerable and in need of care. However, when claims are actually made, 
patients are often denied benefits on the basis of complex, technical, and fine-print 
terms and conditions. These clauses are de liberately drafted in a manner that is 
difficult for an ordinary person to understan d, resulting in exploitation and financial 
distress for consumers. Sir, I urge the Government to take immediate steps to 
regulate both private hospitals and insura nce companies, and to put an end to the 
exploitation of the common ma n. There is an urgent need to plug systemic loopholes 
and ensure transparency and accountability in this sector. Further, I strongly 
recommend that all policy terms and conditio ns must be written in simple language, 
preferably in the mother to ngue of the consumer, so that individuals can fully 
understand their rights and obligations and protect themselves from unfair practices. 
Sir, today, patients are increasingly being treated as mere commodities for profit, with 
private hospitals and insurance companies often acting in collusion, thereby 
compromising access to quality and a ffordable healthcare. Due to such 
circumstances, patients from nearly eight st ates are compelled to seek treatment at 
PGI Chandigarh, leading to excessive burden on the institution and immense hardship 
for patients and their families. Therefore,  I demand that another super-specialty 
hospital be established in this region of Punjab to reduce the load on PGI and improve 
accessibility to quality healthcare. It is the responsibility of the Government to ensure 
adequate medical infrastructure for its ci tizens. At the same time, I would like to 
inform this august House with a sense of pr ide that Punjab has become the first state 
to provide free medical treatment up to ₹10 lakh through empanelled hospitals. I urge 
that such a progressive scheme be replicated across other states for the benefit of the 
wider population. Thank you, Sir.

Statement 
 (a) and (b)  The Government has launched Pradhan Mantri Skilling and 
Employability Transformation through Up graded ITIs (PM-SETU) scheme for the 
infrastructure upgradation of Industrial Tr aining Institutes (ITIs) across the country 
including the State of Uttar Pradesh. The scheme envisages to enhance the overall 
quality and relevance of vocational traini ng with upgraded labs, machines, and 
industry-aligned curriculum in the country. The Scheme has a total outlay of Rs. 
60,000 crores (Central Share – Rs. 30,00 0 crore, State Share – Rs. 20,000 crore 
and Industry Share – Rs. 10,000 crore). 
The key objectives of the scheme are: 
i. To improve the quality of training delivery in ITIs and National Skill Training      
 Institutes (NSTIs); 
ii. To modernize infrastructure and equipment as per industry standards; 
iii.  To introduce industry-aligned long-term and short-term courses, especially 
 in new and emerging sectors; 
iv.  To strengthen industry linkage for demand-driven skilling and better 
 employment outcomes; and 
v. To enhance the capacity of National Skill Training Institutes (NSTIs) for  
 training of trainers. 
The scheme comprises of two components: 
Component I – Upgradation of 1,000 Government ITIs (200 Hub ITIs and 800 
Spoke ITIs) in a Hub and Spoke model wherein upgradation includes smart 
classrooms, modern labs, digital content, and new courses aligned to industry 
needs. 
Component II – Capacity Augmentation of five NSTIs located in Bhubaneswar, 
Chennai, Hyderabad, Kanpur, and Ludhiana, including setting-up sector-
specific National Centres of Excellence for skilling, with focus on advanced 
training of trainers with global partnership.

Under the PM-SETU scheme, industry pa rticipation in curriculum design, 
training delivery and apprenticeship opportunities is strengthened through an 
industry-led governance model. The indust ry-led Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) is 
provided the necessary autonomy to prop ose modifications in the curriculum by 
introducing new courses and upgrading existing courses as per industry 
requirements. The scheme focuses on im proving employability outcomes through 
industry-led governance and aims to enable  learners to acquire industry-relevant 
skills, gain exposure to real work environments, and access career guidance, 
placement support and self-employment opportunities through strengthened 
institutional systems and industry linkages. 
Upgradation of curricula for ITI training programmes is a continuous process 
and is generally undertaken every three ye ars. To meet the demands of the modern 
economy and emerging technologies in the industrial sector, new courses are 
continuously developed and existing cour ses are upgraded in consultation with 
industry, academia and States/UTs. The courses are updated by incorporating new 
technologies and the latest tools, equipm ent and machinery in the curricula, keeping 
in view the requirements of emerging technologies. During the last three years, 14 
Craftsmen Training Scheme (CTS) courses, 15 short-term courses and 07 Flexi-MoU 
courses have been develo ped and approved by National Council for Vocational

Statement 
 (a) The Ministry of women and Child De velopment is the nodal Ministry for the 
administration of Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 (JJ 
Act, 2015) which is the primary legislation for ensuring safety, security, dignity and 
well-being of children and is implemented by all the States an d UTs including the 
State of Uttarakhand. The Act creates statutory structures at the State and District 
levels which include State Child Protection Society (SCPS), State Adoption Resource 
Agency (SARA), Child Welfare Committees (CWCs), Juvenile Justice Boards 
(JJBs), District Child Protection Units (DCPUs ). It also provides for establishment of 
Child Care Institutions (CCIs). 
Under the JJ Act 2015 (Sections 27-30), the Child Welfare Committees 
(CWCs) have been empowered to take decisi ons with regard to the children in need 
of care and protection, keeping their best inte rest in mind. They are also mandated to 
monitor the function of the Child Care Inst itutions (CCIs). As per Section 106 of the 
JJ Act 2015, the primary responsibility for the implementation of the Act lies with 
the State Governments and Union Territory (UT) Administrations. At the national and 
state level, the JJ Act provides the Nati onal/State Commissions for Protection of 
Child Rights to monitor the implementation of the Act (Section 109). 
Inspection Committees are mandated under section 54 of JJ Act, 2015 to visit 
such facilities housing children. District Magist rate is the nodal authority in the district 
for children in need of  care and protection and to take action on the findings of the 
report submitted by the Inspection Committees. The Ministry regularly follows up with 
the State and Union Territory Governments and various advisories have been issued 
so as to ensure the effective implementation of Mission Vatsalya Scheme. 
The Ministry regularly follows up wi th the State and Union Territory 
Governments and various advisories have been  issued so as to ensure the effective 
implementation of Mission Vatsalya Scheme. 
 (b) and (c) The Ministry of Women and Child Development is implementing a 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme, namely ‘Mission Vatsalya’, through the State and UT 
Governments to deliver various services for Children in Need of Care and Protection 
(CNCP) as well as Children in Conflict wi th Law (CCL). These services include 
Institutional Care and Non-Institutional Care.  The Child Care Institutions (CCIs) 
established under the Mission Vatsalya sc heme support, inter-alia, age-appropriate 
education, access to vocational training, recreation, health care, counselling

etc. Under non-institutional care, support is provided to the children through 
Sponsorship, Foster Care, Adoption and After Care. 
As per Mission Vatsalya Guidelines, a CCI having capacity of 50 children can 
have Special Unit for 10 children with sp ecial needs. Similarl y, a CCI having the 
capacity of 25 children can have Special Unit for 5 children. 
The scheme provides for Special Educat ors/therapist and Nurse required for 
such children in CCIs. The Scheme also pr ovides the institutions, inter-alia, with 
specialized equipment and materials like Ps ychological test materials, training 
materials for speech and language, teachi ng materials, wheel chairs. CCIs under 
Mission Vatsalya also provide counselling and psychological support services as a 
standard component of care. Rehabilitation frameworks include individual care plans, 
health services, and emotional support mechanisms. 
The Ministry of Women and Child Deve lopment in collaboration with Lal 
Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Ad ministration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie has 
developed an online training module on Ju venile Justice (Care and Protection for 
Children) Act, 2015 for capacity building of  multiple stakeholders such as State 
Governments and UT Administrations, district  authorities and others. Various training 
and capacity building programmes have been conducted for child protection 
functionaries and other stakeholders across the States and UTs. 
 (d)    Section 41 of the JJ Act, 2015 mandat es every institution which is meant, 
either wholly or partially, for housing ch ildren in need of care and protection or 
children in conflict with law, to be register ed under the Act. The act further provides 
State Governments the power to grant and cancel registration of Child Care 
Institutions which provide rehabilitation an d reintegration services as specified in 
section 53 of the Act. 
 (e)   Mission Vatsalya promotes family ba sed non-institutional care of children 
in difficult circumstances based on the princi ple of institutionalization of children as a 
measure of last resort. Unde r non-institutional care, support is provided to the 
children through Sponsorship, Foster Care , Adoption and After Care. The scheme 
provides Rs.4000/- per month to children  eligible for non-institutional care 
(Sponsorship/ Foster Care/ Aftercare) on cost sharing basis. 
The Ministry has also issued Model Fost er Care Guidelines, 2024 to ensure 
clarity, efficiency and compliance amongst the stakeholders.

To improve the institutional care system, the Government of India has 
supported in establishing the statutory and service delivery structures under Mission 
Vatsalya Scheme, at State and District level namely State Child Protection Society 
(SCPS), State Adoption Resource Agen cy (SARA), Child Welfare Committees 
(CWCs), Juvenile Justice Boards (JJBs), District Child Protection Units (DCPUs) 
and Child Care Institutions (CCIs). Furthe r, under the Juvenile  Justice Amendment 
Act, 2021, the District Magistrates have been made the focal point for the 
administration of JJ Act.

incarcerated parents remain among the most invisible groups in India’s justice 
system. Despite their vulnerability, there is  no reliable national data on how many 
such children exist, their liv ing conditions, or their acce ss to education and welfare.

study notes that as of December 2023, a to tal of 1,492 children were living inside

children, nor does it track outcomes post-i ncarceration. The absence of data itself

standards of care. Additionally, establis h a national database of children of 
incarcerated parents, and ensure coordi nation between prison administration,

Demand for creation of an independent Postal Circle for Goa 
SHRI SADANAND MHALU SHET TANAVADE (Goa) : Sir, I seek to draw attention of 
the Government to a serious administrative issue concerning postal administration in 
Goa. At present, postal services in Go a are administered under the Maharashtra 
Postal Circle. Despite being a separate State with its own distinct identity, Goa 
continues to remain under the administrative control of this circle. While this 
arrangement may have been suitable earlier , it no longer meets present needs, as 
Goa has its own administrative, linguistic and socio-economic requirements. This 
continued dependence on another State’s ad ministrative structure has led to several 
practical challenges. Firstly, recruitment to postal services is conducted at the circle 
level. As a result, candidates from larger  States tend to dominate the selection 
process due to greater competition, thereby limiting fair employment opportunities for 
164
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
 
local youth in Goa and reducing their repr esentation in public service delivery.  
Secondly, many employees recruited from ou tside Goa seek transfers back to their 
parent States after a short tenure, leadin g to recurring vacancies. These vacancies 
are often managed through temporary arrangements, affecting continuity and 
efficiency in postal services. Goa’s small ge ographical size should not be seen as a 
constraint, but rather as an advantage in  creating a more responsive, efficient and 
citizen-centric postal administration. 
I, therefore, urge the Government to co nsider the creation of an independent 
postal circle for Goa. This step will ensu re better administrative control, improve 
service delivery and enhance employment opportunities for local youth in Goa.

Concerns regarding unfair rejection and delay in health insurance claim  
settlements by private insurance companies 
DR. MEDHA VISHRAM KULKARNI (Maharashtra): Sir, I seek to draw the attention of 
the Government to the growing concern re garding the increasing instances of delay 
and unjust rejection of health insuran ce claims by certain private insurance 
companies, causing serious hardship to policyholders across the country. Private 
insurers promote health policies with pr omises of cashless treatment and quick 
settlement of claims. Yet, during medical emergencies many families later find their 
claims partially approved, delayed, or re jected on technical grounds such as pre-
existing disease clauses, documentation issues, or restrictive policy conditions. 
According to the latest annual report of the Insurance Regulatory and Development 
Authority of India, nearly 2.57 lakh complain ts were registered in the insurance sector 
during 2024-25, including about 1.22 lakh related to claim settlement disputes, a large 
share from health insurance. Policyholders have also raised concerns regarding the 
practices of certain insurers where de lays, repeated document requests and 
prolonged verification processes create difficult ies for patients and hospitals. In many

cases, patients enter hospitals expecting insurance coverage, but at the time of 
discharge, families have to arrange large payments due to unresolved claims, placing

settlement managers to coordinate with hosp itals, require transparent disclosure of

OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing away of 
Shrimati Mohsina Kidwai, a former Member of this House, on the 8th of April, 2026, at 
the age of 94 years. She served as the Member of Rajya Sabha representing the State 
of Chhattisgarh for two terms, from 2004 to 2010 and from 2010 to 2016.  
Born on 1st January, 1932 in Banda District of Uttar Pradesh, Shrimati Mohsina 
Kidwai, entered public life at a young age and had a distinguished political career 
spanning over six decades. Over the cour se of her illustrious career, she had the 
distinction of serving in four different le gislatures-both the Houses of Uttar Pradesh 
Legislature and the Houses of Par liament.  Shrimati Mohsina Kidwai also served as a 
Minister in the Government of Uttar Prad esh and as Union Minister holding several 
portfolios. She made significant contribution s to public life and for the upliftment of 
weaker sections of society.  
In her passing away, the nation has lost a veteran legislator, an able 
administrator and a distinguished parliamentarian. 
Hon. Members, with profound grief, I refe r to the passing away of          
Shrimati Asha Bhonsle, one of the most iconic and versatile playback singers of India, 
on the 12th of April, 2026, at the age of 92 years. Born on 8th September, 1933, at 
Sangli in Maharashtra, Shrimati Asha Bhonsle carved an unparalleled niche for herself 
in the world of music and cinema.  With a career spanning over eight decades, she 
lent her melodious voice to thousands of so ngs in multiple Indian languages, leaving 
an indelible mark on the soundscape of Indian music.   
In recognition of her immense contribu tion to the field of music, she was 
honoured with several presti gious awards, including the  Padma 
Vibhushan, Dadasaheb Phalke  Award and National Film Award, in addition to 
numerous national and international accolade s.  She remained an inspiration to 
aspiring artists and a symbol of dedication, excellence and artistic brilliance. 
In her sad demise, the nation has lost a legendary voice, an unparalleled artist 
and a cultural icon whose legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.  We 
deeply mourn the passing away of Shrima ti Mohsina Kidwai and Shrimati Asha 
Bhosle.

REFERENCE BY THE CHAIR 
Achieving of first critic
ality by India’s 500 MW Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor           
at Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu 
MRCHAIRMAN: Hon. Members,  I would like to inform this august House of a 
significant milestone in India’s journey of scientific progress and technological self-
reliance.  On 6th April 2026, at Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu, India achieved an important 
scientific breakthrough. Our 500-Megawatt Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) 
has successfully attained first criticality. This marks the moment when a controlled 
and sustained nuclear chain reaction has been initiated in the reactor. 
Hon. Members, this is not merely a technological milestone; it is a moment of 
national achievement.   Over two decades  in the making, it marks the successful 
culmination of sustained efforts by thousand s of our scientists, engineers, industries 
and multiple units of the Department of At omic Energy.  This historic achievement 
bolsters the Nuclear Energy Mission and streng thens India’s global commitment of 
achieving net-zero emissions by 2070, as a nnounced by the hon. Prime Minister, 
Shri Narendra Modi ji.  The core-loading  of PFBR was also witnessed by the hon. 
Prime Minister in March 2024. 
India’s nuclear strategy is envisioned in three stages to optimise the use of our 
limited Uranium resources and abundant Thor ium reserves.  The first stage currently 
in operation uses natural Uranium in Pr essurised Heavy Water Reactors, producing 
Plutonium as a by-product.   With the real isation of PFBR, India has taken historic 
step of advancing to the second stage. In this second stage, we will utilise Plutonium 
in Fast Breeder Reactors to generate more nuclear fuel. Unlike conventional reactors, 
a Fast Breeder Reactor has the unique capa bility to produce more fuel than it 
[ 16 April, 2026 ]
3

 
 
 
 
consumes. The third stage will be Thorium-Uranium based reactors, enabling a 
sustainable, long-term energy future. 
At a time when India’s energy needs ar e steadily rising and our commitment to 
clean energy is stronger than ever, nuclear  power offers a reliable, round-the-clock, 
low-carbon source of electricity. The House had passed Sustainable Harnessing and 
Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act in December, 
2025 to open up the civil nuclear energy sector to all players. With the whole-of-the-
nation approach, we are steadily marching towards achieving the target of 100 Giga 
Watts of nuclear power.       
 With PFBR attaining criticality, India has entered the second stage of our long-
envisioned programme in civil nuclear ener gy. The PFBR stands as a proud 
testament to India’s long journey of perseverance, innovation and national 
commitment. It serves as a vital bridge, lin king our present capabilities with a more 
sustainable and Atmanirbhar nuclear future.  
This achievement has been made possibl e entirely through indigenous effort. 
The reactor has been designed by the Indi ra Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research 
(IGCAR) and constructed by Bharatiya Nabhikiya Vidyut Nigam Limited (BHAVINI), 
with strong participation from Indian indust ry. It stands as a proud reflection of the 
strength of our scientific ecosystem and the power of national collaboration.  
Hon. Members, with this milestone, India takes its rightful place among a 
select group of nations that have mastered this advanced technology. It reaffirms our 
standing as a nation capable of develo ping and deploying complex, frontier 
technologies with confidence and self-relian ce.  More importantly, it reflects the 
confidence of a nation that believes in its own capabilities and is determined to build a 
future that is secure, sustainable, and self-reliant.  
Looking ahead, the successful operation of PFBR will support the expansion of 
nuclear power in the country and help us move faster towards the third stage of our 
programme. It will also open new opportunities in advanced reactor technologies, fuel 
cycle systems, and high-end engineering.  
Hon. Members, this achievement marks a new beginning -- a beginning that 
carries forward the vision of our pioneers in  science; a beginning that strengthens our 
4
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

 
 
 
 
journey towards energy independence and a be ginning that brings us closer to the 
goal of a Viksit Bharat .   It is also a moment that reaffirms our belief in the power of 
science and technology to shape our co llective future and realise our shared 
aspirations.  
From the first spark of a controlled chain reaction in PFBR emerges not only 
energy, but also the promise of a brighter fu ture for generations to come.  I take this 
opportunity to place on record the appreci ation of this House for the scientists, 
engineers, technicians, industry partners and all stakeholders whose dedication and 
hard work have made this achievement possible.  Thank you.
